Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

thief noun

also thieves, robber, burglar, crook (thief)

classical

Cic. Rosc. Am. 56 (Lewis & Short)
Hor. S. 1.3.106 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 299
Traupman 197, 393

fūr, fūris m./f.

noun, third declension

The thief who steals by stealth; in comedy also a term of abuse, ‘you thief!’ (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • latrō, latrōnis m. — robber, highwayman, bandit

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Hor. S. 1.3.106: nē quis fūr esset, neu latrō (Lewis & Short); Phaedr. 5.2.1; Traupman 196

    One who robs by force, on the road or in a band; in Plautus still a hired soldier (Lewis & Short).

  • fūrunculus, fūrunculī m. — a petty thief, pilferer

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Pis. 66 (Lewis & Short)

    The diminutive of fūr.

  • perfossor, perfossōris m. — housebreaker, burglar

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plaut. (Lewis & Short): perfossor parietum; Traupman 372

    “One who digs through” a house wall; ante- and post-classical (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • nocturnus cum fūr pānem mīsisset canī, objectō temptāns an cibō posset capī

    when a thief in the night threw a dog some bread, trying whether the food would win him overPhaedr. 1.23.3–4

  • 1Varro’s etymology is right: de Vaan 50–51, s.v. arca, derives the noun from the root of arceō, ‘to contain, keep out’.

    arca, quod arcēbantur fūrēs ab eā clausā1

    a chest (arca), because when it was shut thieves were kept off (arcēbantur) from itVarr. LL 5.128

See also steal, crime, prison, police.
